headline_en: Current monetary policy not enough to control inflation
summary_en: At an ICAB roundtable on the January-June 2024 monetary policy, economists and business leaders said the policy will do little to control inflation because the exchange rate is not stable. Several speakers touched on remittances: they cushion rural inflation, remitters get a different dollar rate from exporters, and remittance inflows have fallen. One speaker said students going abroad struggle to buy dollars, often outside banks.

facts.statement: Former state minister for planning Shamsul Alam said on 31 January 2024 at an ICAB roundtable that remittances arriving through both formal and informal channels are keeping the impact of inflation in rural Bangladesh less severe than it would otherwise be.
facts.source_in_article: Shamsul Alam, former state minister for planning

facts.statement: CPD honorary fellow Mostafizur Rahman said in January 2024 that exporters are given one dollar rate while people bringing in remittances are given another rate, which he said has already created discrimination; he argued a 'shock therapy' on the exchange rate would raise both exports and remittance inflows.

DCCI president Ashraf Ahmed said in January 2024 that dollar inflows, including good remittance inflows, were one of the drivers of Bangladesh's growth in recent years, but remittances have now fallen a lot.
facts.source_in_article: Ashraf Ahmed, president, Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry

facts.statement: BUILD CEO Ferdaus Ara Begum said in January 2024 that four different exchange rates are seen in the market, and that people going abroad to study have to struggle to buy dollars, in many cases from outside the banks, adding extra pressure on their parents.
facts.source_in_article: Ferdaus Ara Begum, CEO, Business Initiative Leading Development (BUILD)

facts.statement: Ferdaus Ara Begum of BUILD said in January 2024 that although manpower export (sending workers abroad) is doing well, foreign currency is not coming in to the same extent.
Former ICAB president Jamaluddin Ahmed said in January 2024 that Bangladesh has about 250 authorised money changers but more than 700 businesses are operating in the currency exchange market.

key_quote_bn: যাঁরা দেশের বাইরে পড়তে যাচ্ছেন, তাঁদের কষ্ট করে ডলার কিনতে হচ্ছে। অনেক ক্ষেত্রে এসব ডলার ব্যাংকের বাইরে থেকে নিতে হচ্ছে

headline_en: Canada's two-year cap to cut foreign students by 35 percent; what Bangladeshis should do
summary_en: On 22 January 2024 Canada announced a two-year cap on international student entry, limiting approvals to 360,000 per year, about 35 percent fewer than in 2023, citing a housing crisis. Provinces will set quotas per institution; some provinces may see about 50 percent fewer foreign students, and spouse open work permits are limited to spouses of master's, PhD and postdoc students. The article gives advice to Bangladeshi students on choosing provinces and institutions.

facts.statement: On Monday 22 January 2024 Canada announced a two-year cap on the entry of international students; the immigration ministry said the government decided to approve at most 360,000 students in 2024, about 35 percent fewer than the number admitted in 2023.
facts.source_in_article: Canada's immigration ministry statement; Immigration Minister Marc Miller

facts.statement: Canada said that during the two-year cap period announced in January 2024, issuing work permits to some postgraduate students will be stopped.

Immigration Minister Marc Miller said in January 2024 the cap is not permanent: it will run for the next two years, at 360,000 students per year, and was taken because of Canada's growing housing crisis.

Under the 2024 cap, the federal government in Ottawa will tell each of Canada's 10 provinces and 3 territories its number of foreign students after counting current students; the provinces will then sit with their colleges and universities to set a number for each institution. As of 23 January 2024 the per-province numbers had not been fixed.
Marc Miller said in January 2024 that in some provinces the number of foreign students will fall by about 50 percent under the cap.
Students already studying in Canada whose visa expires before they finish their studies will not fall under the 2024 cap.
Canada has taken steps to reduce foreign students at newly sprung-up small private colleges, which face allegations of low-quality education while bringing in students from around the world.

From the January 2024 announcement, only spouses of students at master's level and above (such as PhD and postdoctoral students) will get an open work permit in Canada; other students' spouses will not be given work permits.

The article advises Bangladeshi students to choose institutions carefully because competition will be high at institutions in Ontario and British Columbia, so they can try provinces other than these two.
The article advises Bangladeshi students to research before choosing a Canadian institution and to pick reputable ones.

The article advises Bangladeshi students who want to stay in Canada after study to finish their studies on time and then start working on a work permit; chasing work instead of studying will make it quite hard to stay on in Canada.

key_quote_bn: মাস্টার্স ও তার ওপরের লেভেলের, যেমন পিএইচডি ও পোস্ট ডক্টরেট শিক্ষার্থীদের স্বামী বা স্ত্রীকে (স্পাউস) শুধু ওপেন ওয়ার্ক পারমিট দেওয়া হবে।

headline_en: Why Bangladesh's growth prospects are shrinking
summary_en: An opinion column by economic analyst Mamun Rashid argues that Bangladesh's growth slowdown to around 4 percent is structural, citing a narrow base (garments and remittances), weak investment climate, weak banks, poor human capital and corruption. On remittances, it says most Bangladeshi migrant workers are unskilled, earn much less per head than workers from competitor countries, and their earnings go mostly to family consumption and land or flats.

facts.statement: Economic analyst Mamun Rashid wrote in a November 2026 Prothom Alo column that remittances are the second pillar of Bangladesh's foreign currency earnings after garments (which bring over 80 percent of export income), a concentration that leaves the economy exposed to external shocks.

Mamun Rashid wrote in November 2026 that because most Bangladeshi migrant workers are unskilled, their per-head income is much lower than that of workers from competitor countries, and most of the remittance income is spent on family consumption and unproductive things like land and flats rather than long-term productive capital.
Mamun Rashid wrote in November 2026 that Bangladesh's growth is now around 4 percent, and that a stable remittance flow is still one of the country's strengths.

key_quote_bn: আমাদের অধিকাংশ অভিবাসী শ্রমিক অদক্ষ হওয়ায় প্রতিযোগী দেশগুলোর তুলনায় তাদের মাথাপিছু আয় অনেক কম।

headline_en: Let foreign relations serve our own interests, on our own terms
summary_en: An opinion piece by Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah (University of Brunei Darussalam) argues Bangladesh should pursue strategic autonomy among India, China and the United States and diversify partners. In passing it says relations with Southeast Asia and the Gulf must go beyond sending workers, that migrant workers' fair wages, safety and legal protection should be central in Gulf bilateral talks, and suggests skilled employment and worker protection cooperation with Malaysia.

facts.statement: Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah wrote in a November 2026 Prothom Alo opinion piece that Bangladesh needs a specific programme with Malaysia on skilled employment and worker protection, and that relations with Southeast Asia should go beyond sending workers and official visits.
facts.source_in_article: A K M Ahsan Ullah, professor, international security and migration, University of Brunei Darussalam

facts.statement: A K M Ahsan Ullah wrote in November 2026 that relations with the Gulf countries should go beyond sending workers and buying energy, and that economic cooperation will be meaningful only when migrant workers' fair wages, safety and legal protection become central topics of bilateral talks.

A K M Ahsan Ullah suggested in November 2026 that Bangladesh can build issue-based alliances with like-minded countries on migrants' rights, climate compensation, refugee burden-sharing and ocean resources.

key_quote_bn: অভিবাসী শ্রমিকের ন্যায্য মজুরি, নিরাপত্তা ও আইনি সুরক্ষা দ্বিপক্ষীয় আলোচনার কেন্দ্রীয় বিষয়ে পরিণত হবে।

headline_en: Visible digital seal could reduce visa document fraud
summary_en: At a seminar in Gulshan, Dhaka on 8 November 2026, Bangladeshi company Relief Validation Limited (RVL) promoted its Visible Digital Seal (VDS), a PKI-signed 2D code on documents that breaks if any part is altered and can be checked with the VeriQR app. RVL's CEO said visa refusal rates for Bangladeshis are rising because foreign missions cannot quickly verify easily forged bank statements, certificates and salary papers. Germany's ambassador said forged or unverifiable documents in a few applications force officials to scrutinise every application.

facts.statement: Relief Validation Limited (RVL) CEO Rashed Mahmud said on 8 November 2026 that visa refusal rates for Bangladeshi applicants in various countries are steadily rising, and that the main cause is not the applicants but a lack of trust in their documents.
facts.source_in_article: Rashed Mahmud, CEO, Relief Validation Limited

facts.statement: Rashed Mahmud of RVL said in November 2026 that bank statements, certificates and salary documents submitted with Bangladeshi visa applications are easy to forge while foreign missions cannot verify them quickly, so because of some fraudsters every applicant faces extra scrutiny and genuine students and workers get refused.

Bangladeshi company Relief Validation Limited (RVL), headquartered in Gulshan, Dhaka, offers a Visible Digital Seal (VDS): a digitally signed two-dimensional code, signed with public key infrastructure (PKI), added to paper or PDF documents; even a small change to the document breaks the seal, and after sealing even the issuing institution cannot change the data.

A Visible Digital Seal on a document can be verified within seconds by any authority in any country using the VeriQR app, without emailing or phoning the issuing institution; it shows who issued the document, whether data was changed and whether it is valid.

RVL said in November 2026 that its Visible Digital Seal is already used by various banks, universities and government institutions in Bangladesh, and that it can be used on medical certificates, police clearance certificates, insurance documents and marriage certificates needed for visa and immigration applications.

German ambassador to Bangladesh Rüdiger Lotz said on 8 November 2026 that because a small number of visa applications contain forged or unverifiable documents, officials have to examine every application far more closely than normal, taking more time and effort; he said technology like VDS could help decisions be made faster.
facts.source_in_article: Rüdiger Lotz, German ambassador to Bangladesh

named_actors.name: Relief Validation Limited (RVL)
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Bangladeshi company offering Visible Digital Seal document verification technology to reduce visa document fraud; CEO Rashed Mahmud.

key_quote_bn: ব্যাংক বিবরণী, সনদ ও বেতন-সংক্রান্ত কাগজপত্র জাল করা সহজ হলেও বিদেশি মিশনগুলো দ্রুত এসব নথি যাচাই করতে পারে না।

headline_en: Why Gen Z's destination is abroad
summary_en: A feature by a BRAC University student explains why Bangladeshi Gen Z increasingly go abroad, citing admission competition, quality of education, unemployment and, for women, safety and freedom. It gives figures on students abroad (UNESCO), student spending abroad (Bangladesh Bank), unemployment (BBS, IMF), Canada's 2026 seat limit, 51 Bangladeshi students at Japan's Saga University, and RMMRU's 2025 worker migration count.

facts.statement: According to UNESCO, about 52,800 Bangladeshi students were in higher education abroad in 2023, up from a little over 24,000 in 2013, more than double in a decade.
facts.source_in_article: UNESCO data, cited in the article

facts.statement: According to Bangladesh Bank, students sent more than USD 660 million (66 crore dollars) abroad for study in fiscal year 2024-25.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank, cited in the article

facts.statement: According to the BBS Labour Force Survey 2024, Bangladesh had 2.46 million (24 lakh 60 thousand) unemployed people in 2023, rising to about 2.62 million (26 lakh 20 thousand) in December 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics Labour Force Survey 2024

facts.statement: According to the September 2026 issue of the IMF's Finance and Development magazine, about 36 percent of Bangladesh's post-secondary educated youth labour force aged 15 to 24 are unemployed.
The article says that on average 36 candidates compete for each seat at Bangladesh's public universities, which pushes some students to go abroad right after HSC.
Canada has kept only 155,000 (1 lakh 55 thousand) seats for new international students in 2026.

The article says that as complexity and costs rise in the United States and Canada, many Bangladeshi students are now considering countries in Asia and Europe such as Germany, Italy, Finland, South Korea and China, and that the number of students learning various languages in Dhaka is growing fast.
In 2026, 51 Bangladeshi students went to Saga University in Japan, for the first time the university's largest group of foreign students.

The article lists the steps for studying abroad as a set IELTS score, an admission letter, bank statement, sponsor's papers and then a visa interview, with waiting at each step and risk of failure at the last step, plus country-specific restrictions.
facts.source_in_article: the article; student Jannatul Ferdous Tripti also lists IELTS, SOP, bank statement and sponsor papers

facts.statement: According to a report by migration research organisation RMMRU, 1,130,757 (11 lakh 30 thousand 757) workers went abroad from Bangladesh in 2025.
facts.source_in_article: RMMRU report, cited in the article

facts.statement: A 2021 German study of 5,408 first-semester university students found 25 percent of female students expressed a clear intention to go abroad for higher education versus 20 percent of male students.
facts.source_in_article: a 2021 study in Germany, cited in the article

facts.statement: Tasmim Binte Karim Omi, a Bangladeshi student in Saint John, Canada, who left four years earlier after HSC, said the biggest challenge abroad was handling every situation alone and not finding like-minded people to socialise with; she had not been able to visit home once in four years.
facts.source_in_article: Tasmim Binte Karim Omi, student in Canada

people_cases.what_happened: Went abroad for higher education four years earlier after HSC, fearing failure in the university admission competition at home; has not returned home in four years.
people_cases.outcome: Says she gained personal freedom, better education and living; biggest challenge is loneliness and handling everything alone.

people_cases.who: Jannatul Ferdous Tripti, final-year student, Criminology and Police Science, University of Chittagong
people_cases.what_happened: Preparing IELTS, SOP, bank statement and sponsor papers; says only three universities in Bangladesh offer her subject.

key_quote_bn: কানাডা ২০২৬ সালে নতুন শিক্ষার্থীর জন্য রেখেছে মাত্র ১ লাখ ৫৫ হাজার আসন।

headline_en: Prime Minister's visit: our expectations from the Land of the Rising Sun
summary_en: An opinion column by Dhaka University economics professor Sayema Haque Bidisha on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to Japan discusses USD 6.35 billion of Japanese investment interest, the February 2026 Bangladesh-Japan EPA and the BIG-B initiative. It argues Japan's ageing population creates a large labour market opportunity for Bangladesh that has not been used due to policy failures, and calls for affordable Japanese language training in districts, transparent government-supervised recruitment, ending middlemen, cheaper migration and labour market analysis.

facts.statement: During Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's October 2026 visit to Japan, Japan and Japanese entrepreneurs showed interest in investing USD 6.35 billion over the next five years in Bangladesh's private sector (automobile, other manufacturing, power plants), which could create 200,000 (two lakh) jobs.
facts.source_in_article: bilateral talks between the two prime ministers, as reported in the column

facts.statement: A Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) was signed in February 2026, covering bilateral trade, investment and support on LDC graduation; its implementation was a priority in the October 2026 talks.

Professor Sayema Haque Bidisha wrote in October 2026 that because a large share of Japan's population is elderly, Japan's labour market (ageing-related worker shortages and elderly care) is a big opportunity for Bangladesh as a young country, but it has not been used well because of policy, diplomatic and administrative failures, lack of coordination and lack of policy continuity.
facts.source_in_article: Sayema Haque Bidisha, professor of economics, University of Dhaka (opinion)

facts.statement: Sayema Haque Bidisha recommended in October 2026 affordable, easy Japanese language training in various divisions and certain districts chosen by demand, plus training in interpersonal skills and job-related information, noting that without quality education and training the whole recruitment process for Japan will be hampered.

Sayema Haque Bidisha wrote in October 2026 that a government-led ecosystem around training centres should ensure job information, a transparent recruitment process under government supervision, an end to middlemen and brokers, affordable migration costs and links with Japanese employers, and that Japan's labour market should first be analysed by sector, qualification and skill demand.
About 340 Japanese companies operate in Bangladesh, and Japan's share of Bangladesh's garment exports rose to 3.25 percent in July-September of the current fiscal year.

key_quote_bn: জাপানের জনগোষ্ঠীর একটি বড় অংশ বয়স্ক হওয়ায় বার্ধক্যজনিত শ্রমিক-সংকট ও বয়স্কদের সেবা কার্যক্রমের জন্য তরুণ জনগোষ্ঠীর দেশ হিসেবে বাংলাদেশের একটি বড় সুযোগ রয়েছে।

headline_en: Two Bangladeshis executed: parliamentary committee asks whether the Bangladesh consulate failed
summary_en: On 25 October 2026 the parliamentary standing committee on the foreign ministry asked whether the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah was weak or negligent over the execution of two Bangladeshis in Makkah; the ministry said Saudi Arabia had sent a list of about 2,500 prisoners 14 days before the execution that included their names, but it was not properly identified. The committee also discussed abuse of women workers in Saudi Arabia: the ministry said 1-2 percent of about 169,000 Bangladeshi women workers there face abuse and 1,364 women domestic workers have been rescued and repatriated.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's foreign ministry told the parliamentary standing committee on 25 October 2026 that, 14 days before two Bangladeshi nationals were executed in Makkah, Saudi Arabia had sent a list of about 2,500 prisoners that included the two men's names, but the matter was not properly identified.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign ministry, to the parliamentary standing committee

facts.statement: The foreign ministry told the committee in October 2026 that, based on the prisoner category shown in the Saudi list, officials thought the two Bangladeshis might get 6 months to 15 years in jail and did not understand they would be executed.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign ministry, to the parliamentary standing committee

facts.statement: The parliamentary standing committee on the foreign ministry, chaired by Zahurat Adib Chowdhury, asked on 25 October 2026 for a report on whether the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah was weak or negligent over the two executions, what action was taken, and what is being done to prevent a repeat; the ministry has sent Saudi Arabia questions (a separate report says six questions) and was asked to share the answers.
facts.source_in_article: Parliamentary standing committee; Zahurat Adib Chowdhury

facts.statement: The foreign ministry told the parliamentary committee in October 2026 that about 169,000 (1 lakh 69 thousand) Bangladeshi women workers are currently in Saudi Arabia, and that 1-2 percent of them are victims of abuse.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign ministry, as relayed by committee chair Zahurat Adib Chowdhury

facts.statement: The foreign ministry's figure on abuse of Bangladeshi women workers in Saudi Arabia comes from asking women when they come for passport services and from a third-party survey.

The foreign ministry reported in October 2026 that 1,364 Bangladeshi women domestic workers have been rescued and safely repatriated from Saudi Arabia; committee chair Zahurat Adib Chowdhury said this number is not acceptable even if 1-2 percent sounds small.
facts.source_in_article: Zahurat Adib Chowdhury, citing the foreign ministry

facts.statement: The parliamentary committee directed the foreign ministry in October 2026 to take steps to bring abuse of Bangladeshi women workers in Saudi Arabia to zero and recommended necessary steps to protect women workers in Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries.

headline_en: From the Dhaka-Toronto experience, the prospects of Dhaka-New York
summary_en: A US-based academic describes flying Biman Bangladesh Airlines Toronto-Dhaka in August 2026: Biman's Toronto office did not answer phones, and large excess-baggage charges were demanded, including BDT 20,000-25,000 from students going to Canada for one pound of excess weight at Dhaka. He argues for more cabin crew and a Dhaka-New York route for Bangladeshis in the US.

facts.statement: A columnist reports that on his return trip from Dhaka in about August-September 2026, Biman Bangladesh Airlines staff were collecting BDT 20,000-25,000 from students going to study in Canada for just one pound of excess baggage weight.
The columnist says that at Biman's counter at Toronto airport in August 2026 he was asked to pay several hundred dollars extra for being even one pound over the baggage limit.

The columnist says he phoned Biman Bangladesh Airlines' Toronto office several times during office hours in August 2026 to ask about an extra bag and its cost, but the automated system kept transferring calls to station manager, country manager and other officers and no one answered.

The columnist says Biman's Dhaka-Toronto flight stops in Rome, Italy, takes about 20 hours, was completely full, and is used by many Bangladeshis from New York state cities such as Buffalo, Albany and Rochester; cabin crew told him about 80 percent of the route's income comes from cargo.
facts.source_in_article: Dr Delwar Arif; Biman cabin crew

facts.statement: The columnist says a Biman Toronto-Dhaka flight some time before August 2026 had a mechanical fault before its Rome stopover, causing passengers long suffering, and that he chose Biman partly to avoid Middle East airspace because of the Iran war.

named_actors.name: Biman Bangladesh Airlines
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Toronto office did not answer customer calls; staff charged large excess baggage fees, including BDT 20,000-25,000 from students for one pound over.

headline_en: Sent to the battlefield 'as bait': SRB says 17 Bangladeshis died in drone attacks on the first day
summary_en: The Special Response Battalion (SRB) said on 14 October 2026 that 30 Bangladeshis went to Russia on 7 May 2026 through Jabale Noor International, RS International and TS Group, each paying about BDT 10 lakh for promised construction jobs, but had passports and phones taken and were handed to the Russian army, sent to the Russia-Ukraine front after 21 days' training. SRB has confirmed at least 20 deaths, 17 on the first day from drone attacks; the men were used as bait to locate enemy positions. Jabale Noor founder Mizanur Rahman and Abu Taher alias Lentu were arrested.

facts.statement: On 7 May 2026, 30 Bangladeshis went to Russia through three firms, Jabale Noor International, RS International and TS Group, having been told they would work at construction companies; each paid on average about BDT 10 lakh.

After the 30 Bangladeshis reached Russia in 2026, their passports and mobile phones were taken, they were not given the promised construction jobs, and they were handed over to the Russian army, given 21 days of military training and sent into the Russia-Ukraine war.

SRB said in October 2026 that the 30 Bangladeshis were deployed in three groups (front, middle and rear); 17 died in drone attacks on the very first day and three more deaths were reported later, so 20 of the 30 are preliminarily confirmed dead.

SRB-10 commander Additional DIG Moha. Asaduzzaman said on 14 October 2026 that the Bangladeshis were not fit for war and had no physical, training or tactical preparation, and that SRB understood they were sent to the battlefield as a kind of bait so that when the enemy hit them with drones, Russia could identify the attackers' position and distance.
facts.source_in_article: Additional DIG Moha. Asaduzzaman, commander SRB-10

facts.statement: Of the survivors among the 30 Bangladeshis, two returned to Bangladesh injured; of the other eight, two are under treatment in a Moscow hospital and six are still on the battlefield, as of October 2026.
Survivor Rajon said a drone strike on the battlefield broke his hip and paralysed his lower body, and he crawled on his chest about four kilometres to reach the camp; he has returned to Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Rajon, survivor, as relayed by SRB

facts.statement: SRB arrested Mizanur Rahman (55), founder of Jabale Noor International and one of the leaders of the human trafficking ring, and Abu Taher alias Lentu over sending Bangladeshis to the Russian army; efforts were under way to arrest another member, Mostafizur.
facts.source_in_article: SRB press conference, Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, 14 October 2026

facts.statement: SRB said a Russian man named Igor and a Kyrgyz woman named Julia were involved in the trafficking alongside the Bangladeshi ring; information collection and operations against them were ongoing.

SRB said people from many countries have been drawn into Russia's war the same way, and from Bangladesh people went especially from Gopalganj, Mymensingh, Narayanganj, Jamalpur, Pabna, Chapainawabganj, Faridpur, Rajbari and Gazipur.
SRB said most victims are from poor families, some went abroad on loans, and many families who got news of a relative's death have no chance to see the body or bring it home.
SRB's Moha. Asaduzzaman urged people lured by overseas jobs to verify the legitimacy of the firm involved before paying money or travelling.
A related headline in the article notes that the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on a Bangladeshi company over alleged human trafficking to Russia.

headline_en: Prime Minister urges Canada to cooperate in health, education and other sectors
summary_en: On 12 October 2026 Prime Minister Tarique Rahman met a Canadian delegation led by Minister of State for International Development Randeep Sarai and asked Canada to help in health, education and technology. Canada expressed interest in energy supply, technical and vocational education and training, food security and feasibility studies; Sarai praised Bangladeshis living in Canada and noted two Bangladeshi-origin Canadians are MPs. The PM's adviser on expatriates' welfare and overseas employment, Mahdi Amin, attended.

headline_en: Stopped from going abroad: the three women describe what happened at the airport
summary_en: Three unmarried women stopped by immigration police at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 8 August 2026 while travelling to Nepal with valid passports, visas or entry permission and tickets gave statements to a police inquiry on 8 October 2026. They allege police phoned their parents, made offensive remarks about clothes, finances and personal matters, kept one passport, gave no written reason, and one officer said they were not allowed to go because they were unmarried. They had complained to an Additional IGP on 30 August and the High Court on 29 September ordered the complaint resolved.

facts.statement: On 8 August 2026 three unmarried women travelling to Nepal for tourism from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, with valid passports, visas or entry permission and air tickets, were stopped by airport immigration police after collecting boarding passes and were sent out through the arrival terminal.
facts.source_in_article: the three women's statements to police

facts.statement: One of the three women says that when she asked why they were being sent out on 8 August 2026, an immigration police member told them they were not being allowed to go because they were unmarried; another said an immigration police member told her unmarried girls cannot go abroad alone.

The women say immigration police at Dhaka airport took them from the terminal desk to an office, phoned their parents to ask whether they knew their daughter was going abroad and about the parents' occupations, asked about the source of travel money, asked one to call her university dean, made offensive remarks about clothes, a hijab photo on a student ID and a Nepali name on the hotel booking, and kept one woman's passport.
The women say no written document was given to them when they were turned away at Dhaka airport on 8 August 2026.

One woman says she carried a boarding pass, valid passport, hotel booking and dollar endorsement for the Nepal trip; the women also had return tickets and said no NOC from their internship employer was required for them.
facts.source_in_article: the women's statements and answers to police

facts.statement: The three women complained to the Additional Inspector General of Police on 30 August 2026 seeking an inquiry and action; with no result they filed a writ, and on 29 September 2026 the High Court issued a rule and ordered the complaint resolved.

After the High Court order, a three-member police committee was formed, and on Thursday 8 October 2026 the three women gave statements and were questioned for about six hours at the relevant office in Rajarbagh, Dhaka.
One woman says her father, a farmer whom police phoned and asked how a farmer's daughter could travel abroad, was traumatised by the incident, had an accident on 17 August 2026 and later died.

headline_en: Expelled Jubo Odhikar leader who said 'it must be five, VP Nur's order' arrested; extortion case filed
summary_en: Lakshmipur district DB police arrested Faruk Hossain, expelled president of the district Jubo Odhikar Parishad, on 5 October 2026 after a leaked audio in which he demanded money from a person wanting to go abroad for passport work, visa, police clearance and BMET card, invoking the name of expatriates' welfare state minister Nurul Haque Nur; a party source said he demanded BDT 5 lakh. An extortion and BDT 10 crore defamation case was filed on 6 October. Faruk denies it, saying the audio was AI-edited and he asked BDT 5,000 for a passport.

facts.statement: In an audio recording that spread on social media on 5 October 2026, Faruk Hossain, then president of Lakshmipur district Jubo Odhikar Parishad, is heard demanding money from a person wanting to go abroad as initial costs for passport work, visa, police clearance and BMET card, saying 'it must be five, this is VP Nur's order'; a party source said he demanded BDT 5 lakh for these.
facts.source_in_article: the leaked audio; a party source

facts.statement: Lakshmipur district Detective Branch (DB) police arrested Faruk Hossain on the night of Monday 5 October 2026; on 6 October 2026 at about 3:30 pm former district Gono Odhikar Parishad general secretary Solaiman Chowdhury filed a case at Lakshmipur Sadar police station against him and several unnamed others for extortion and BDT 10 crore defamation.
facts.source_in_article: the article; OC Mohammad Wahid Parvez, Lakshmipur Sadar police station

facts.statement: Lakshmipur Sadar OC Mohammad Wahid Parvez said the case against Faruk Hossain is for seeking money by using the name of Nurul Haque Nur, Gono Odhikar Parishad president and state minister for expatriates' welfare; DB police are investigating.
Faruk Hossain denied the allegation, claiming a local ring made the audio by editing his voice with AI, and said he did not ask for BDT 5 lakh but for BDT 5,000 to get a passport made.

Expatriates' welfare state minister Nurul Haque Nur wrote on Facebook in October 2026 that no one will escape by running scams using his name, and that the accused had been expelled and the Lakshmipur superintendent of police asked to take legal action.

headline_en: Jordan to take 300 machine operators through government channel, jobs by direct interview
summary_en: BOESL will recruit 300 female garment machine operators for Jordan through the government channel by direct interview on 25 September 2026 at the Bangladesh Korea Technical Training Centre, Mirpur, Dhaka. Basic monthly pay is USD 183.61 (about BDT 22,587), age 20-35, application fee BDT 100 online; the three-year renewable contract includes employer-provided housing, food, first aid, transport and air fares both ways.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) announced in September 2026 that 300 female machine operators will be recruited for garment factories in Jordan through the government channel, by direct interview.

For BOESL's September 2026 Jordan garment machine operator (female) jobs, age limit is 20-35 years, and certificate holders trained in the relevant trade at BMET-run technical training centres get priority.
Basic monthly salary for BOESL's September 2026 Jordan female garment machine operator jobs is USD 183.61 (about BDT 22,587), with eight hours of duty a day, six days a week, and voluntary overtime.

The BOESL Jordan garment job contract (September 2026) is for three years, renewable; the employer provides accommodation, food, first aid and transport, and pays the air fare to join and the return air fare after three years.

Application for BOESL's September 2026 Jordan machine operator jobs is made through the website with an application fee of BDT 100; no fee is payable to BOESL until the worker is finally selected, and all fees and charges must be paid through a bank.
The direct interview for BOESL's Jordan female machine operator jobs was held on 25 September 2026 at 8 am at the Bangladesh Korea Technical Training Centre, Darus-Salam Road, Mirpur, Dhaka-1216.
A related headline in the article says there are government-channel jobs in Brunei, with 279 people to be recruited.

headline_en: Oman expatriate arrested with weapons; family claims he was framed
summary_en: Police in Senbag, Noakhali arrested Md Jabed Hossain (30), an Oman-based expatriate home on leave for about one and a half months and due to return the next week, in a night raid on 6-7 September 2026, claiming to recover a pipe gun, a cartridge and two machetes. His family and the local UP chairman say he was framed, possibly over a land dispute; police say the raid was based on specific information and a fair investigation will be done.

facts.statement: Police arrested Oman-based expatriate Md Jabed Hossain (30) of Bishnupur village, Nabipur union, Senbag upazila, Noakhali, at about 2:30 am after Sunday night (6 September 2026), claiming to recover a pipe gun, a cartridge and two machetes from his bedroom; he was sent to court on Monday under an Arms Act case.

facts.statement: Jabed Hossain had come home from Oman about one and a half months earlier and was due to return to his workplace the next week; his wife Farhana Akter says he runs a business in Oman, has no criminal past, and may have been framed by a rival party in a land dispute, noting their door was found open that evening.
facts.source_in_article: Farhana Akter, wife; Nabipur UP chairman Md Belayet Hossain Sohel

facts.statement: Noakhali Superintendent of Police N M Nasir Uddin said he asked the OC to look into the discussion about the arms recovery from the expatriate's house, and the OC said whether there is any confusion around the raid will be examined through a fair and impartial investigation.
facts.source_in_article: SP N M Nasir Uddin; OC Abdur Rahim Sarkar
